subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Ascaris lumbricoides is a large intestinal roundworm that spreads via contaminated food or soil. It can cause intestinal blockage, lung migration, and anemia. Diagnosis relies on stool eggs and clinical clues, and treatment is with albendazole or mebendazole.

sections.p: A soil‑transmitted helminth, Ascaris lumbricoides is the largest human roundworm, often found in tropical and subtropical regions. It thrives in warm, moist soils contaminated with human feces.
The adult worm is up to 35 cm long, with a thick cuticle and a prominent buccal capsule. Eggs are oval, 50–70 µm, and contain a larval stage that can survive in soil for years.

t.b: Identify oval eggs with bipolar plugs; confirms infection

sections.p: Infection occurs when eggs are ingested from contaminated food, water, or soil. Eggs hatch in the intestine, larvae penetrate the gut wall, migrate to the lungs, ascend the trachea, and are swallowed back to the gut to mature.

t.b: Eggs may be intermittent, repeat testing improves yield

sections.p: Ascariasis can be asymptomatic or cause abdominal pain, malnutrition, intestinal obstruction, and pulmonary symptoms during larval migration. Severe cases may lead to perforation or death.

t.b: Severity graded by symptom intensity and imaging

sections.p: Diagnosis is clinical plus laboratory confirmation. Stool microscopy is the gold standard; serology is not routinely used. Imaging (X‑ray, ultrasound) helps assess obstruction.

t.b: Negative does not rule out; repeat 3 times

sections.p: First‑line therapy is albendazole or mebendazole, chosen for efficacy and low toxicity. Supportive care includes hydration, pain control, and monitoring for complications. Mass deworming and sanitation reduce transmission.

t.b: Avoid in pregnancy; monitor for hepatotoxicity

sections.p: Remember the life cycle: ingestion → intestinal larva → lung migration → cough (Löffler’s syndrome) → re‑ingestion. Key diagnostic test is stool microscopy; repeat if initial negative. Treatment is albendazole; avoid praziquantel as it is ineffective.
b: Life cycle: ingestion → lung migration → re‑ingestion

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with vomiting (possible obstruction), persistent cough with wheeze, signs of anemia or shock
